theory.overview: Shortest path algorithms find the minimum cost path between nodes in a weighted graph. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a single source with non-negative weights (O(E log V)). Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles (O(VE)). Floyd-Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths (O(V³)). A* uses heuristics for faster search in known spaces. These power GPS navigation, network routing, and game AI pathfinding.

keyConcepts.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
keyConcepts.description: Greedy algorithm using priority queue. Maintains tentative distances, always processes closest unvisited node. Only works with non-negative weights.

keyConcepts.name: Relaxation
keyConcepts.description: Core operation: if path through u improves distance to v, update v's distance. Repeated until no improvements possible.

keyConcepts.name: Negative Weights
keyConcepts.description: Negative weights can create negative cycles (infinite negative distance). Bellman-Ford detects these; Dijkstra fails silently.

keyConcepts.name: A* Search
keyConcepts.description: Dijkstra + heuristic estimate to goal. f(n) = g(n) + h(n). With admissible heuristic, finds optimal path faster.

complexity.dijkstra: O(E log V) with binary heap

algorithmSteps.description: Dijkstra: Initialize distances. A is source (distance 0). Priority queue = [A]
Process A: Relax neighbors. B=4, C=2. Add to PQ.
Process C (closest): Relax D. A→C→D = 2+1 = 3. Better than ∞!
Process B: B→D = 4+5 = 9. Not better than current D=3.
Process D: No outgoing edges. Algorithm complete!
Final shortest paths from A: B=4, C=2, D=3 (via C)
